moves.spoken: Black transposes into a Dutch with f5, but a London player doesn't change course — keep playing the standard London moves.
Think about what f5 costs Black: it weakens the a2-g8 diagonal and makes castling awkward — if we react correctly.
moves.teaches: The Dutch f5 concedes the a2-g8 diagonal; punish it before Black consolidates.

moves.spoken: So we break our own routine: Bc4 instead of the usual Bd3 or Be2. This is a schematic opening, but when the opponent deviates you must think outside the setup — Bc4 seizes the diagonal f5 just weakened and slows his castling.
moves.teaches: In a system opening, abandon the automatic move when the opponent's play demands a concrete reaction.

moves.spoken: He struggles to play e6, and we keep the Ng5 jump in our pocket — but don't rush it, just finish developing patiently.
moves.teaches: Bank a strong idea for later; complete development before cashing it in.

moves.spoken: h3 is a typical London move, reserving the h2 retreat for the bishop.
Now expand on the queenside with c4. Yes, it blunts our own bishop for the moment — but the plan is a later c5, which reopens the diagonal and cranks up the queenside pressure.
moves.teaches: Temporarily blocking your own bishop is fine when a later break reopens it with interest.

moves.spoken: Nc3 develops and points us toward the c5 or e4 break — either one gets at the e6-pawn.
moves.plans: Prepare c5 or e4 to open lines against e6.

moves.spoken: Rc1 is playing for your future self — not an immediate threat, but the rook wants to be on the c-file long before c5 ever lands.
moves.teaches: Place pieces for the break you'll make later, not only for the threat you can make now.

moves.spoken: Here's the deep plan: c5 is much easier with a pawn on b4 first.
moves.plans: Reroute so you can push b4, then break with c5.

moves.spoken: But b4 fails right now — the bishop on b3 would have to go to c2, off the diagonal, dropping the c4-knight. The fix, learned from a painful loss: play a3 first, tuck the bishop back to a2, then send the pawn forward.
moves.teaches: When a pawn break needs a square a piece occupies, reroute the piece first, then push.

moves.spoken: c5 breaks through. Don't fear him carving out d5 — the square is firmly held by our bishop and knight, so a knight can't settle there.
moves.teaches: A pawn break is safe to make when your pieces already blanket the hole it concedes.

moves.spoken: And there's the payoff of reopening the diagonal: Bxe6-check slices straight through, and we simply help ourselves to the free pawns.
moves.teaches: The point of opening a bishop's diagonal is the sacrifice-free tactic waiting at the end of it.

moves.spoken: To convert, note Black has no light bishop, so build a queen-and-bishop battery down the light squares — queen in front, since it's the queen that delivers mate on h7. And don't hurry to grab the knight on f6: it isn't going anywhere, Black stays permanently weak on the diagonal, so improve elsewhere and open a file with f4 to pile on.
moves.teaches: Against a king with no light bishop, stack a light-square battery led by the queen at h7, and never rush a capture the target can't flee.
